excerpt: When a driver has a heart attack or seizure at the wheel, the sudden medical emergency defense may block liability. When it applies, and when it fails.
keyTakeaways: The sudden medical emergency defense allows drivers to avoid liability for accidents caused by unforeseeable medical events like heart attacks, seizures, and strokes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, the burden falls on the driver to prove the episode was genuinely unforeseeable. The defense fails when the driver had prior episodes, doctor's warnings, or untreated conditions. Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) apply. Even if the defense succeeds, coverage that pays regardless of fault (MedPay, optional PIP, health insurance) may still apply, and in South Carolina a medical provider who failed to warn the driver about impairing treatment may be liable; Georgia does not recognize that claim. UM/UIM applies when the driver is liable but uninsured or underinsured.

faqs.question: What is the sudden medical emergency defense?
faqs.answer: The sudden medical emergency defense is a legal doctrine that may shield a driver from liability if they caused an accident due to an unforeseeable loss of consciousness or physical incapacitation. Common examples include heart attacks, seizures, strokes, and diabetic emergencies. The driver invoking this defense bears the burden of proving the event was genuinely unforeseeable.

faqs.question: Can I still sue if the other driver had a heart attack while driving?
faqs.answer: Possibly. The key question is whether the medical event was foreseeable. If the driver had a known heart condition, prior episodes, or doctor's warnings about driving, the sudden emergency defense may fail. In South Carolina you may also have a claim against a medical provider who failed to warn the driver that treatment could impair driving; Georgia does not allow that claim against a non-patient's doctor. Your own UM/UIM coverage applies if the driver is liable but uninsured or underinsured.

faqs.question: Who has the burden of proof in a sudden medical emergency case?
faqs.answer: The driver who caused the accident bears the burden of proving the medical emergency was unforeseeable and that they lost consciousness or physical control. This is different from typical personal injury cases where the injured person proves the other driver's negligence. Both Georgia and South Carolina place this burden on the defendant.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for these cases in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations for personal injury claims is 2 years from the date of the accident under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. This applies regardless of whether the at-fault driver raises a sudden medical emergency defense. If you miss the deadline, you lose the right to file a claim.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina allows 3 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Medical malpractice claims against a prescribing doctor have a separate 3-year statute with a discovery rule. Acting promptly preserves evidence and strengthens your case.

faqs.question: What insurance options do I have if the driver is not liable?
faqs.answer: If the at-fault driver successfully proves a sudden medical emergency, coverage that pays regardless of fault may still apply: MedPay, personal injury protection (PIP) if you purchased it (neither state requires it), and health insurance. Uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage pays only what you are legally entitled to recover from the other driver, so it applies when the driver is liable but uninsured or underinsured. An attorney can review all available coverage to maximize your recovery even when the other driver escapes liability.
